query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated experimental–simulation approach that separately quantifies lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr will achieve a predictive accuracy improvement of approximately 20–30% compared to earlier models based on defect‐free bulk crystal approximations and simplified Debye treatments.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy in a pristine, homogeneous state with minimal contamination, and a variant with 1 wt.% oxygen doping.
generation.intervention: Apply a combined method that couples advanced DFT-based phonon Boltzmann transport calculations (incorporating full anharmonic lattice dynamics) with explicitly resolved experimental measurements using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) for lattice contributions and Hall measurements for electronic contributions.
generation.conditions: Measurements and simulations are conducted over a wide temperature range from 200 K to 1200 K. Experiments are performed on both pristine samples (to isolate intrinsic lattice transport at low temperature) and oxygen-doped (1 wt.% O) samples at high temperatures to mimic realistic defect-induced scattering.
generation.structural_mediator: Incorporation of atomic-scale defects and microstructural disorder into DFT simulations, alongside in situ experimental techniques that distinguish between phonon and electron carriers.
generation.mechanism: Separately calculating lattice transport using anharmonic phonon dynamics and capturing electronic transport via direct measurements avoids the oversimplifications of the Debye model and defect-free assumptions. This separation enables precise tuning of simulation parameters to reflect experimentally observed scattering mechanisms and microstructural complexities.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity components that, when combined, show a total thermal conductivity within 20–30% lower uncertainty relative to previous predictions. At temperatures below 200 K, the lattice contribution should dominate, while at higher temperatures (300–1200 K) the electronic contributions become comparable or more significant, matching or improving upon observed values (10–17 W/(K m) in oxygen-doped specimens).
generation.baseline: Earlier approaches using ideal, defect-free bulk crystal simulations and Debye approximations that conflated lattice and electronic contributions.
generation.boundary: The predictive improvement is expected to hold for high-entropy alloys under controlled laboratory conditions in the specified temperature range; extreme environments or significant deviations from the assumed microstructural disorder may limit the model's applicability.
generation.uncertainty: While the integrated approach is supported by analogues in similar HEA systems (e.g., PbSnTeSe studies), the exact magnitude of improvement (20–30%) in predictive error may vary. Deviations could arise due to unaccounted defect states or interfacial phenomena between phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples (one pristine and one with 1 wt.% oxygen). Perform in situ TDTR measurements to separately determine the lattice thermal conductivity and Hall measurements to determine the electronic contributions across the temperature range 200–1200 K. Conduct parallel DFT-based simulations incorporating full anharmonic lattice dynamics and explicit defect modeling to predict separate contributions.
measurements: Temperature-dependent lattice thermal conductivity via TDTR
Electronic thermal conductivity via Hall effect measurements
Comparison of predicted vs. measured separate contributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined predicted thermal conductivity (with separated lattice and electronic components) deviates by more than 20–30% from the experimental values across the reported temperature range, or if the low-temperature regime (<200 K) does not show the expected dominance of lattice transport relative to electronic transport, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, PbSnTeSe has been experimentally investigated by Fan et al. [] and Raphel et al. [,], who report appreciably similar results for the thermoelectric performance of the material (see below). The modelling of HEAs transport properties constitute a challenge, and both the simulation methods and their derived predictions have to be confronted to experimental data to assess their validity. In this context, we present in this paper for the first time a complete approach that allows one to obtain all the transport coefficients, including the figure of merit, of a high-entropy alloy. The thermoelectric transport properties of the PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloy have been calculated by combining state-of-the-art methods based on the special quasi-random structures approach to generate the HEA structure, the first-principles density-functional theory (DFT), and the Boltzmann transport and Green–Kubo theories. First, from the DFT-computed material electronic states, the electronic transport properties (electronic conductivity, Seebeck coefficient and electronic thermal conductivity) were calculated using the linearized Boltzmann transport equation, and the power factor was obtained. chosen.lever: Explicit separation of lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity
chosen.technique: Integrated experimental approach (time‐domain thermoreflectance and electronic transport measurements) combined with DFT‐based simulations that independently compute lattice and electronic transport
chosen.conditions: Focused on HfNbTaTiZr samples across 200–1200 K, including low-temperature regimes (<200 K) for isolated lattice/electronic behavior and oxygen-doped specimens (1 wt.% O) at high temperatures
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by unifying experimental data with atomistic simulations, overcoming previous limitations of idealized, defect-free models and simplified analytical approaches. It is expected to outperform earlier methods by reducing predictive error by approximately 20–30%, and its dual-range (low and high temperature) comparisons with established measurements offer clear, falsifiable benchmarks.
